L5A  /  Pathological basis of oral & systemic disease

Hypersensitivity Reactions

Immunopathology Part 1. The immune system doing exactly what it was built to do, and injuring the host in the process. Four mechanisms, three of them antibody-driven and one cell-driven — and two of them can kill a patient in your chair.

Lecturer
Dr Joseph Ryan
Sections
21
Core reading
Underwood’s Ch. 8
Builds on
L3B immune system
01

What hypersensitivity is

Damage caused not by the pathogen, but by the response to it.

Hypersensitivity reaction

Incidental tissue injury as a result of the immune response intended to destroy foreign antigens.

Read that definition carefully, because the whole lecture turns on the word incidental. The immune response is doing what it is designed to do. The damage is collateral — a side effect of a response that is either aimed at the wrong target, out of proportion to the threat, or unable to stop.

Where this sits in the unit

Lecture 3B built the immune system: antibodies, MHC, T cells, B cells, macrophages. This lecture is what happens when that machinery injures the host. Every mechanism here is one you have already met — only the outcome is different.

02

Causes of hypersensitivity reactions

Three sources of the antigen that sets it off.

Cause 1

Autoimmunity

The response is directed at a self antigen. Covered in full in Part 2.

Cause 2

Microbes

Three ways: an excessive reaction; a persistent microbe, e.g. Mycobacterium tuberculosis; or cross-reactivity with a self antigen, e.g. rheumatic heart disease.

Cause 3

Environmental antigens

In some genetically susceptible individuals. 20% of the population are allergic to certain substances.

Atopy

An inherited tendency for overproduction of IgE antibodies to common environmental antigens. Note that atopy is the tendency, not the disease — it is the inherited predisposition that makes type I reactions likely.

High yield

Rheumatic heart disease is the classic cross-reactivity example: antibodies raised against streptococcal antigens also bind cardiac tissue because the two are structurally similar. The immune system has not malfunctioned — it cannot tell the two apart. That is molecular mimicry, and it returns in Part 2 as a cause of autoimmunity.

03

The four types

Gell and Coombs — three antibody-mediated, one T cell-mediated.

TypeNameMediated byCore event
IImmediate hypersensitivityIgE on mast cellsAntigen cross-links IgE → mast cell degranulation
IIAntibody to cell-bound antigenIgM or IgGAntibody binds an antigen fixed to a cell membrane
IIIImmune complex reactionsIgG + complementAntibody binds a soluble antigen → complexes deposit
IVDelayed hypersensitivityT cellsSensitised T cells react on re-exposure, 2–3 days later
The organising split

Types I, II and III are antibody-mediated. Type IV is cell-mediated. That single division explains almost every difference between them — including why type IV is the only one that is delayed. Antibody is already circulating and acts in minutes; T cells must migrate to the site, which takes days.

Types II and III are both IgG-mediated. What actually separates them?

Where the antigen is. In type II the antigen is part of a cell membrane, so the antibody binds the target cell directly and the damage is confined to tissues carrying that antigen. In type III the antigen is soluble; antibody and antigen form immune complexes in the circulation, which then deposit in blood vessels, joints and glomeruli — so the damage occurs wherever the complexes lodge, not where the antigen came from.

04

Type I: the mechanism

Six steps from first exposure to late-phase damage.

Often called allergy or atopy. The most common disorder of the immune system.

  1. Initial exposure
    Antigen (e.g. pollen, peanuts, penicillin) activates a strong TH2 response — either a protein antigen, or a chemical that binds to a protein antigen.
  2. Class switching to IgE
    IL-4 and IL-13 released by the TH2 cell cause the B cell to activate and switch to an IgE-releasing plasma cell, producing IgE targeted against that antigen.
  3. Mast cell sensitisation
    IgE binds the Fc receptor on mast cells. Mast cells sit in all connective tissues, especially under epithelia and close to blood vessels — which is exactly where an inhaled or ingested allergen will arrive.
  4. Repeat exposure cross-links IgE
    Antigen binds two or more IgE molecules on a previously sensitised mast cell. That cross-linking is the trigger.
  5. Immediate reaction
    Vasoactive amines — histamine causes dilation of blood vessels, increased vascular permeability and contraction of smooth muscle. Proteases damage local tissue.
  6. Late phase reaction
    Cytokines recruit lymphocytes. Eosinophils and neutrophils release proteases which cause further tissue damage.
Why the first exposure causes nothing

Steps 1–3 are sensitisation and are clinically silent. The patient who reacts violently to a drug has almost always had it before. This is why "he's had penicillin before without trouble" is not reassurance — it is the precondition.

05

Type I: the cytokine sequence

Three interleukins, three jobs.

The lecture sets the sequence out as: allergen inhaled, ingested or injected → activation of Th2 cells → release of three interleukins, each with a distinct role.

CytokineAction
IL-4Stimulates B cells to undergo class switching to IgE, and to produce IgE
IL-5Activates eosinophils
IL-13Stimulates mucus secretion in epithelial cells
Keeping them apart

4 makes IgE (four letters, IgE-four). 5 feeds eosinophils. 13 makes mucus. Between them they account for the three things an allergic patient shows: specific IgE on testing, eosinophilia on bloods, and a running nose.

From the lecture slides
06

Mast cell sensitisation

The receptor worth knowing by name.

Sensitisation of mast cells is by IgE. IgE binds the Fc portion of the ε chain on mast cells — the receptor is FcεRI, also found on basophils and eosinophils. Once IgE is bound, the mast cell is “sensitised” and will degranulate the next time that antigen appears.

Straight from Lecture 3B

You met the Fc region as the constant stem of the antibody that binds cell receptors. This is that mechanism in action: the Fc end anchors IgE to the mast cell, leaving both Fab arms free and pointing outwards, ready to catch antigen. The class of heavy chain (ε = IgE) is what determines which receptor it can dock with.

Why cross-linking matters

A single IgE molecule binding antigen does nothing. The signal requires antigen to bridge two or more adjacent IgE molecules, clustering their receptors. This is why very small quantities of a multivalent allergen can trigger a massive response, and why a monovalent hapten alone generally cannot.

From the lecture slides
07

Mast cell mediators

Preformed in the granules, then newly synthesised.

Preformed mediators — released on degranulation

MediatorEffects
HistamineVasodilation, increased vascular permeability, smooth muscle contraction, and increased secretion of mucus
ChemokinesAttract neutrophils and eosinophils
ProteasesTissue damage, generation of kinins, activation of complement — causing further chemotaxis and inflammation

Newly synthesised mediators

MediatorEffects
Prostaglandin D2The most abundant mediator generated by the cyclooxygenase pathway in mast cells. Causes intense bronchospasm and increased mucus secretion
Leukotrienes LTC4, LTD4The most potent vasoactive and spasmogenic agents known — several thousand times more active than histamine at increasing vascular permeability and causing bronchial smooth muscle contraction
Leukotriene LTB4Highly chemotactic for neutrophils, eosinophils and monocytes
Why do antihistamines fail to control severe asthma or the late phase of an allergic reaction?

Because histamine is only one preformed mediator. The leukotrienes LTC4 and LTD4 are several thousand times more potent than histamine at increasing vascular permeability and contracting bronchial smooth muscle, and PGD2 causes intense bronchospasm. These are newly synthesised rather than preformed, so they act later and are not blocked by an H1 antagonist.

08

Complement in hypersensitivity

Why activating complement makes everything worse.

Mast cell proteases activate complement, and complement then amplifies the reaction. The lecture lists its biological effects:

  1. Lysis of antigen, opsonisation and phagocytosis
    The intended, protective functions.
  2. Release of pro-inflammatory mediators C5a, C4a and C3a
    These increase vascular permeability, release vasoactive amines and induce smooth muscle spasm — the same three effects as histamine, from a second source.
  3. C5a is a potent chemoattractant
    Pulling further inflammatory cells into the site.
Why this matters across all four types

Complement is the common amplifier. It appears in type II (antibody bound to a cell fixes complement and lyses it), in type III (immune complexes fix complement, which is what makes the deposits injurious), and here in type I. Wherever antibody meets antigen in quantity, complement turns a local event into an inflammatory one.

09

Anaphylaxis: recognising it

The one type I reaction that will kill someone in your chair.

Anaphylaxis

Sudden hypotension, severe bronchoconstriction and collapse. A type I hypersensitivity reaction. Common triggers: bee and wasp venom, antimicrobials, peanuts, latex. The word is Greek for “backwards protection”.

Anaphylactoid reactions

The same mast cell mediators are responsible, but the stimulus for their release does not depend on IgE. Clinically identical, so treated identically — but because there is no IgE step, it can happen on first exposure, with no prior sensitisation.

In dental practice

Incidence is quoted at 0.004 to 0.015 cases per dentist per year — rare enough that you may never see one, frequent enough that you must be ready. Causative agents in dental practice include latex, topical preparations (povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine) and oil of cloves.

Clinical presentation by system

SystemFeatures
SkinUrticaria, angioedema, pruritus
RespiratoryStridor, wheezing, shortness of breath, upper airway angioedema, persistent cough
CardiovascularHypotension, syncope, cardiac arrhythmias, tachycardia
CNSUnconsciousness, dizziness, confusion, headache
GITNausea, vomiting
Chlorhexidine — a documented dental killer

Chlorhexidine causes both type I and type IV reactions. The lecture is explicit: type I anaphylactic reactions have been reported where tooth sockets were irrigated with chlorhexidine, resulting in fatalities. Irrigating a socket puts CHX directly into an open vascular bed.

From the lecture slides
10

Anaphylaxis: management

Adrenaline, by autoinjector, without delay.

DeviceDoseUse
EpiPen or Anapen300 µg adrenalineStandard adult / child over 5
EpiPen Jr or Anapen 150150 µg adrenalineUnder 5 years of age
Anapen 500500 µg adrenalineSome patients are prescribed this
The one instruction to remember

Repeat administration every 5 minutes if symptoms persist. A single dose is not the treatment — it is the first dose. Call for an ambulance at the same time.

Why adrenaline and not an antihistamine

Adrenaline reverses the three things killing the patient: it causes vasoconstriction (opposing the hypotension), bronchodilation (opposing the bronchospasm), and it stabilises mast cells. An antihistamine blocks only one mediator, after it has already bound. In anaphylaxis the leukotrienes alone would be enough to kill.

A patient collapses after you irrigate an extraction socket with chlorhexidine. What has happened, and what do you do?

Most likely anaphylaxis — a type I hypersensitivity reaction to chlorhexidine, which is a documented cause of fatalities when sockets are irrigated with it, because the drug enters an open vascular bed. Give adrenaline by autoinjector (300 µg for an adult), call an ambulance, and repeat the adrenaline every 5 minutes while symptoms persist.

From the lecture slides
11

Type II: antibody to cell-bound antigen

The antibody binds something that is part of a cell.

Antibodies react with antigenic determinants which form part of the cell membrane on the target tissue. IgM or IgG are typically implicated, and the reaction may involve complement and/or accessory cells.

Three ways type II antibodies cause damage

Mechanism 1

Direct inflammatory attack

Antibodies target self-antigens directly, causing an inflammatory reaction specific for the tissues which harbour that antigen — e.g. mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP).

Mechanism 2

Opsonisation

Antibodies opsonise cells such as red blood cells, causing phagocytosis of the cell — e.g. autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.

Mechanism 3

Receptor interference

Antibodies bind receptors and either inhibit their function or mimic the ligand, activating the receptor.

DiseaseTargetResult
Myasthenia gravisAcetylcholine receptorAntibody inhibits neuromuscular transmission → paralysis
Graves diseaseTSH receptorAntibody activates thyroid function without TSH being present
The pair worth memorising

Myasthenia gravis and Graves disease are the same mechanism with opposite signs: one antibody blocks a receptor, the other stimulates it. Because Graves disease stimulates rather than destroys, it is sometimes classified separately as type V hypersensitivity — the lecture notes this explicitly.

From the lecture slides
12

Type II: drugs and bystander lysis

The commonest way you will cause a type II reaction.

Many involve drugs or their metabolites which have bound to the surface of red blood cells or platelets to form highly immunogenic epitopes. The antibody is raised against the drug, but the drug is stuck to a cell — so the cell is destroyed with it.

Bystander lysis

Antibodies formed against the drug or its metabolite inadvertently destroy the cell as well. The cell has done nothing wrong; it simply happened to be what the drug attached to.

Haemolytic anaemia Thrombocytopenic purpura

The same mechanism operates in autoimmune disorders where the target antigen is intrinsic — there is no drug involved, the self antigen was always there. Autoantibodies can bind to the functional sites of self-antigens, such as receptors for hormones or neurotransmitters, blocking their action.

Dental relevance

Mucous membrane pemphigoid is the type II disease you will meet in the mouth: autoantibodies against components of the basement membrane zone produce sub-epithelial blistering, desquamative gingivitis and scarring. It is the direct-attack mechanism above, with the oral mucosa as the tissue that harbours the antigen.

13

Type III: immune complexes

Soluble antigen, so the damage happens somewhere else entirely.

Antibodies target soluble antigens, forming immune complexes which fix complement and are not cleared from the circulation. Those complexes then deposit in blood vessels, joints and glomeruli, and the deposits induce a localised inflammatory response causing tissue damage.

The defining feature

In type II the antibody goes to the antigen's tissue. In type III the complex travels and lodges wherever the circulation narrows — which is why type III diseases are characteristically multi-system, hitting vessels, joints and kidneys regardless of where the antigen came from.

What happens where they deposit

  1. High concentration of immune complexes
    Deposited in the vessel wall or basement membrane.
  2. Complement activation
    The complexes fix complement, generating C3a and C5a.
  3. Platelet aggregation
    Contributing to local vascular obstruction.
  4. Neutrophil attraction
    Drawn by C5a; they release enzymes onto the deposit.
  5. Local inflammation
    And with it, tissue damage.

When complex formation becomes chronic

Chronic immune complex formation and deposition occurs in persistent antigen exposure, abnormal immune response by the host, or local defects, e.g. in complement function.

From the lecture slides
14

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

A worked example — and a lesson in timing.

  1. A streptococcal infection of the throat or skin
    The antigen source.
  2. 10–12 days pass
    Time for antibody to be raised and complexes to form.
  3. Antigenic fragments bind the glomerular basement membrane
    From certain ‘nephritogenic’ strains of streptococci.
  4. Deposition of immune complexes of IgG and C3
    In the glomerular basement membrane.
  5. Inflammation and renal injury
    The kidney is damaged by a response to an infection that was in the throat.
A ‘one-shot’ mechanism

The lecture calls this a ‘one-shot’ mechanism — a single burst of complex formation following one infection, rather than the continuous deposition seen in SLE. That is why it typically resolves once the antigen is cleared, whereas SLE relapses indefinitely.

The 10–12 day gap is the point

The delay is not incidental — it is diagnostic. The kidney disease appears after the sore throat has resolved, which is precisely why the two were not connected for so long. If a question gives you a latent period of about a fortnight after a streptococcal infection, it is asking about type III.

15

Systemic lupus erythematosus

The multi-system type III disease, with oral signs.

SLE is characterised by multisystemic inflammation resulting from abnormal immune function, with periods of flares and periods with no observable signs. It is a type III hypersensitivity reaction: immune complexes deposit in tissue, activating the complement system, resulting in inflammation and tissue damage.

Four types of lupus

1

Systemic (SLE)

Multisystem disease.

2

Neonatal

In the newborn.

3

Discoid

Limited to skin and oral mucosa; chronic scarring and atrophic dermatoses which may progress to SLE.

4

Drug-induced

Follows exposure to medication and resolves on cessation — generally within days to weeks, but can take months.

Epidemiology

Incidence (US)2–8 per 100,000
Prevalence (Australia)45 per 100,000 — higher in Indigenous Australians
SexFemale predominance; most common in females of child-bearing age

Aetiology

Multifactorial; the exact process is unknown.

  • Genetics — over 100 genetic loci associated with SLE, each giving a small increased risk, generally in pathways altering immune function. 25% concordance in monozygotic twins, 2–5% in dizygotic twins.
  • Environmental — EBV, UV light and smoking implicated, with case reports of hair dyes and many other triggers. The belief is that an environmental trigger initiates an abnormal immune response.
  • Female predominance — possibly endocrine.

Clinical presentation

SystemFeatures
SkinButterfly (malar) rash, photosensitivity; occasionally alopecia, Raynaud’s phenomenon
MusculoskeletalArthralgias, myalgias, arthritis
PulmonaryPainful breathing, coughing, shortness of breath
CardiovascularPericarditis, myocarditis, endocarditis, coronary artery disease
GITNausea, vomiting, abdominal pain
HaematologicalAnaemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia
Diagnosis — the numbers

There is no consensus criteria set; the American College of Rheumatology 1997 classification criteria are used diagnostically. 11 criteria; 4 of 11 are considered diagnostic, of which one must be clinical and one immunological. Sensitivity 95%, specificity 85%.

Anti-nuclear antibodies are almost always positive in SLE, but are not specific. Anti-Sm and anti-dsDNA are highly specific; anti-C1q is associated with disease activity.

The malar rash detail

The classic butterfly rash covers the cheeks and nasal bridge and characteristically spares the nasolabial folds. That sparing is the distinguishing feature — it is what separates it from rosacea and from a photosensitive dermatitis.

Why is a positive ANA test insufficient to diagnose SLE?

Because anti-nuclear antibodies are almost always positive in SLE but are not specific to it — they occur in other autoimmune conditions and in healthy people. Diagnosis uses the ACR 1997 criteria: 4 of 11, with at least one clinical and one immunological item. The specific markers are anti-Sm and anti-dsDNA, with anti-C1q tracking disease activity.

From the lecture slides
16

Type IV: delayed-type hypersensitivity

No antibody at all — and that is why it takes days.

  1. T cells sensitised by primary exposure
    The silent sensitising step, as in type I — but the memory is held in T cells, not IgE.
  2. Secondary challenge
    Followed by a delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) reaction.
  3. T lymphocytes react with antigen
    Releasing IL-2, IFN-γ and other Th1 cytokines.
  4. Takes 2–3 days to develop clinically
    Because circulating effector T cells must migrate to the site of antigen — the lecture gives 24–48 hours for that migration.
  5. Infiltrate
    T lymphocytes, macrophages and occasional eosinophils.

Major causes

Cause 1

Autoimmunity

Type I diabetes, multiple sclerosis.

Cause 2

Environmental antigens

An exaggerated or persistent reaction — e.g. contact dermatitis, viral hepatitis.

Which T cell does the damage

CellAction
CD4+React against self antigen, releasing cytokines that initiate localised inflammation and activate macrophages. Th1 cells release IFN-γ, recruiting macrophages; Th17 cells release IL-17, recruiting neutrophils. These are the main effector cells causing tissue damage
CD8+React against self antigen directly, killing those cells
BothIn some conditions, both CD4+ and CD8+ cells may be present
Link to Lecture 3B

The macrophage–lymphocyte loop you drew for chronic inflammation is this mechanism. IFN-γ from Th1 cells activating macrophages is exactly how a granuloma is sustained — which is why tuberculosis is both a chronic granulomatous infection and a type IV hypersensitivity reaction. Same biology, two labels.

Why is type IV the only delayed type, when types II and III also take hours to days?

Because type IV requires cells rather than antibody to reach the site. Antibody in types II and III is already circulating and binds as soon as it meets antigen. In type IV, sensitised effector T cells must migrate to where the antigen is, which takes 24–48 hours, with the reaction clinically evident at 2–3 days and most visible at 48–72 hours.

From the lecture slides
17

Type IV in the mucosa

Six steps — the version that matters for oral lesions.

  1. Antigen uptake and presentation
    Antigens are taken up by Langerhans cells, which travel to the lymph node and present them in conjunction with MHC-II to CD4+ cells. This creates memory CD4+ cells.
  2. Subsequent exposure
    Stimulates the sensitised CD4+ cells to secrete cytokines.
  3. Adhesion molecules upregulated
    TNF-α and TNF-β stimulate ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 on the endothelial cells of blood vessels.
  4. Extravasation
    Enabling neutrophils, monocytes and macrophages to leave the vessel.
  5. Tissue damage
    Increased capillary permeability contributes to oedema; enzymes from macrophages contribute to tissue damage and necrosis.
  6. Peak and decline
    The reaction is most visible after 48–72 hours, and periodically diminishes after that.
Two familiar things reappearing

Langerhans cells are the antigen-presenting cells of epithelium, and ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 are the adhesion molecules from the leukocyte emigration cascade in Lecture 3A. The margination–adhesion–diapedesis sequence is identical — only the trigger differs.

18

Contact dermatitis

The everyday type IV reaction.

Certain occupational and other antigens are not immunogenic on their own. They are highly reactive molecules that bind to skin and tissue molecules — a hapten becoming immunogenic only once coupled to a carrier protein.

Pathogenesis: two phases

Phase 1

Induction

Langerhans cells in the skin bind and present the hapten–carrier complex to T lymphocytes in association with MHC class II — usually months after exposure to small amounts of antigen.

Phase 2

Elicitation

On re-exposure, effector T cells migrate to the skin to meet the protein complex presented by Langerhans cells in the epidermis, with consequent cytokine release and skin inflammation.

Irritant versus allergic

Contact dermatitis can be irritant or allergic. Only the allergic form is a type IV hypersensitivity response. Irritant dermatitis is direct chemical damage with no immune memory — which is why it can occur on first contact and in anyone, whereas allergic contact dermatitis requires prior sensitisation.

Clinical features

Dermatitis occurs 12–48 hours after contact with the allergen. Papular erythematous plaques, scaling and loss of skin integrity including fissures, in the distribution of exposure, with poorly defined margins. The hands are most commonly involved, but the face, lips and eyelids are commonly affected too.

Histopathology

Spongiotic reaction pattern Keratinocytes separated by oedema Lymphocyte exocytosis Superficial perivascular infiltrate: eosinophils + lymphocytes

Chronic exposure may lead to epithelial hyperplasia.

Management

  1. Avoidance of the allergen
    The definitive treatment.
  2. Patch testing
    To confirm which allergen.
  3. Skin care
    Avoid detergents on affected skin; rehydrate with aqueous cream or petroleum jelly.
  4. Topical steroids
    Mild topical steroids may be used. Acute contact dermatitis of the face may require short-term oral corticosteroids.
19

Oral contact allergy

The dental version — and the materials you will be handling.

A type IV reaction affecting the oral mucosa. It may present as oral lichenoid reactions, which are considered separately.

Symptoms

What the patient reports

Burning, stinging and/or tingling sensations in the oral mucosa, xerostomia, dysgeusia and other sensory disturbances.

Signs

What you see

Erythema, oedema, desquamation, ulceration, often affecting the tongue, gingiva and/or lining mucosa. May also present with cheilitis and peri-oral inflammation.

Common materials

GroupExamples
Restorative materialsAmalgam, resins, acrylics
MetalsGold sodium thiosulfate, nickel sulphate, amalgam alloy components, mercury, chromium–cobalt, palladium chloride
Flavouring agentsCinnamon, peppermint, spearmint, fragrance mix, balsam of Peru
Other toothpaste componentsCocamidopropyl betaine, propylene glycol, parabens, sodium laureth sulphate, triclosan

Contact allergy to toothpaste

Uncommon, and less common than it once was, because formulations changed to remove the offending ingredients — particularly cinnamon. The most common presentation is cheilitis, which may occur without any intra-oral involvement: dry lips, erythema, swelling, cracking, mild fissuring and/or angular cheilitis.

The diagnostic catch

The most common allergen is flavouring, often listed only as “unspecified flavouring” on the ingredient list — so the label may not let you identify it. Patch testing can support the diagnosis but will not always confirm it, and a positive result may not be clinically significant. The lecture's recommendation is the stop–restart method: withdraw the product, see if it resolves, reintroduce, see if it recurs.

Diagnosis and treatment

  1. Establish a temporal relationship
    Between onset and any of the substances above.
  2. Assess
    Patient-reported symptoms, physical examination findings, and patch testing of suspected contact allergens.
  3. Remove the cause
    Replace restorations. Change oral hygiene products.
  4. Symptomatic control
    Topical steroids may be needed.
  5. If chlorhexidine anaphylaxis
    EpiPen to administer adrenaline, and call emergency for an ambulance.
Chlorhexidine does both

Chlorhexidine is known to cause both type I and type IV reactions. A patient with a burning mouth after a CHX rinse is showing type IV; a patient collapsing after socket irrigation is type I. The same agent, two entirely different mechanisms and two entirely different responses.

A patient develops burning and desquamation of the tongue two days after a new toothpaste. What is the mechanism, and how would you confirm it?

Oral contact allergy — a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction, consistent with the 12–48 hour onset. The likely allergen is a flavouring agent, historically cinnamon, and it is often listed only as “unspecified flavouring”. Confirmation is best by the stop–restart method, since patch testing will not always confirm it and a positive result may not be clinically significant.

20

Patch testing

How a type IV allergy is demonstrated.

  1. Apply the suspected sensitiser
    To normal skin on the patient’s back, and cover for 48 hours.
  2. Inspect at 2 and 4 days
    The reaction site is read twice.
  3. Read the response
    A positive response shows inflammation and induration at the test site.
Why the timings are what they are

The 48-hour occlusion and the 2- and 4-day readings exist because this is a delayed reaction — effector T cells need 24–48 hours to migrate, and the response is most visible at 48–72 hours. Reading a patch test at 20 minutes would tell you nothing, which is precisely how patch testing differs from the skin-prick testing used for type I allergy.

Test to type

Type I → skin prick test, read in minutes, looking for a weal and flare. Type IV → patch test, read at 2 and 4 days, looking for induration. If a question tells you which test was used, it has told you the type.

From the lecture slides
21

Summary and glossary

The whole of Part 1 on one screen.

The through-line

  1. Hypersensitivity is incidental damage
    The immune response is working; the injury is a side effect.
  2. Three antibody types, one cell type
    I, II and III are antibody-mediated; IV is T cell-mediated, and that is why only IV is delayed.
  3. Type I is IgE on mast cells
    Sensitisation is silent; cross-linking on re-exposure triggers immediate and late-phase mediators.
  4. Type II binds a cell-bound antigen
    Direct attack, opsonisation, or receptor block/stimulation.
  5. Type III binds a soluble antigen
    Complexes travel and deposit — hence multi-system disease.
  6. Type IV needs T cells to arrive
    2–3 days; the mechanism behind contact allergy and oral contact allergy.
  7. Two dental emergencies to know
    Chlorhexidine anaphylaxis after socket irrigation, and adrenaline repeated every 5 minutes.

Glossary

Hypersensitivity reaction
Incidental tissue injury as a result of the immune response intended to destroy foreign antigens.
Atopy
An inherited tendency for overproduction of IgE antibodies to common environmental antigens.
Sensitisation
The clinically silent first exposure during which IgE or memory T cells are generated.
FcεRI
The receptor binding the Fc portion of the IgE ε chain, on mast cells, basophils and eosinophils.
Preformed mediators
Histamine, chemokines and proteases, stored in mast cell granules and released immediately.
Newly synthesised mediators
PGD2 and leukotrienes, made on demand; responsible for the late phase.
Anaphylaxis
Sudden hypotension, severe bronchoconstriction and collapse; a type I reaction. Greek for “backwards protection”.
Anaphylactoid
Clinically identical to anaphylaxis, but mediator release does not depend on IgE.
Bystander lysis
Destruction of a cell by antibody raised against a drug bound to its surface.
Immune complex
Antibody bound to soluble antigen, which may fix complement and deposit in tissues.
Nephritogenic strain
A streptococcal strain whose antigenic fragments bind the glomerular basement membrane.
Malar rash
The butterfly rash of SLE over cheeks and nasal bridge, characteristically sparing the nasolabial folds.
ANA
Anti-nuclear antibodies — almost always positive in SLE, but not specific.
Anti-dsDNA / anti-Sm
Autoantibodies highly specific for SLE.
DTH
Delayed-type hypersensitivity; the type IV reaction, clinically evident at 2–3 days.
Hapten
A small molecule that is not immunogenic alone but becomes so when bound to a carrier protein.
Induction phase
Langerhans cells present the hapten–carrier complex on MHC II, sensitising T cells.
Elicitation phase
On re-exposure, effector T cells migrate to the skin and cause inflammation.
Spongiosis
Separation of keratinocytes by oedema — the histological pattern of contact dermatitis.
Patch test
Suspected sensitiser applied to back skin for 48 hours, read at 2 and 4 days; positive shows inflammation and induration.
Type V hypersensitivity
Sometimes used for stimulatory autoantibody disease such as Graves.
Required reading

Underwood’s Pathology: a Clinical Approach (8th ed.), Simon Cross, Chapter 8 — Immunology and Immunopathology: hypersensitivity reactions.
